ui.own_warn: Above {max} you are past the largest rise this comparison was built around. The model still works it out, but only by assuming customers keep reacting in the same straight-line way to a bigger rise — nothing here shows that they do. Treat this figure as rough.
ui.sheet_link_note: This link carries the figures you entered — sales, costs, cash. Anyone you send it to can read them. They sit after the # in the link, so opening it does not send them to the web server.
ui.test_overlap: The ranges overlap because the model is also unsure how fast customers react. A result inside an overlap cannot tell the settings apart, and small daily counts widen it further. An unclear result is a normal outcome.
ui.test_need: What to record: every day, how many of the repriced items you sell and how many of a few similar items you did not reprice — for a week before and at least two weeks after. Keep the same days and hours, and avoid weeks with promotions, holidays or stock-outs.
ui.test_need_capacity: What to record: requests for the repriced services and for your other services — not bookings, which your diary caps — for two weeks before and at least four weeks after. Keep the same days and hours, and avoid weeks with promotions or holidays.
ui.test_days_l: How many days ago did you raise it?
ui.test_n_l: How many days does each average cover?
ui.test_oth_h: Similar items you did not reprice (strongly recommended)
ui.test_oafter_l: Daily {unit} in the same latest days
ui.test_c1: Same opening days and hours in both periods
ui.test_c2: No promotion, holiday or special event in either period
ui.test_c4: Nothing else changed at the same time — other prices, the menu, staff, suppliers
ui.test_status_supported: Your test points to “{band}”, and it met every condition. The comparison now uses “{band}”.
ui.test_status_provisional: Your test points to “{band}”, but not every condition was met, so the comparison still uses what it used before. Keep it as a note.
ui.test_status_inconclusive: Your test fits more than one setting ({bands}), so it cannot tell them apart and nothing was changed. That is a normal result, not a failure.
ui.test_status_outside: Your result does not fit any setting we tested. Something else probably changed during the test — or your customers react differently from every setting here. Nothing was changed.
ui.test_status_legacy: Recorded with an earlier version of this test that did not check its conditions. Kept as a note; the comparison does not use it.
ui.test_obs: What you saw: after a {rise} rise, daily sales of the repriced items changed by {t}, comparing the latest {n} days (up to day {days} after the change) with before.
ui.test_obs_ctl: What you saw: after a {rise} rise, daily sales of the repriced items changed by {t} and of the unchanged items by {o}, comparing the latest {n} days (up to day {days}) with before. Against the unchanged items, that is {rel}.
ui.test_obs_legacy: Recorded then: after a {rise} rise, every 1% on the price went with about {v}% fewer sales.
ui.test_inf: What the model infers, under its own assumptions about how fast customers react: this fits “{bands}”.
ui.test_inf_none: What the model infers: none of its settings would produce a change like this.
ui.test_open_noctl: No unchanged items were counted, so a quiet or busy fortnight cannot be told apart from the price change.
ui.test_open_checks: Not every condition was confirmed; whatever was different may explain part of the change.
ui.test_open_short_n: Each average covers fewer than 7 days, so weekday patterns can distort it.
ui.test_open_short_days: Fewer than 14 days had passed; under the model's assumptions most of the reaction may still be to come.
ui.test_open_capacity: Your diary is capped by your slots, so fewer bookings may not show until demand falls below them. This test never changes the comparison automatically.
ui.test_open_noise: The range allows only for ordinary counting noise. Real weeks usually vary more, so treat even a clear-looking result with care.
ui.test_open_items: It covers a few items; using it for your whole business is still a judgement.
ui.test_open_legacy: Run the test again with the unchanged items and the checks, and it can be used.
ui.sheet_meas_supported: My own test pointed to “{band}”, and the comparison above uses that setting.
ui.sheet_meas_other: I ran a test with a {rise} price rise. Its result was {state}, so the comparison above does not rely on it.
ui.test_state_provisional: provisional — not every condition was met
ui.test_state_inconclusive: inconclusive — it fitted more than one setting

cafe.question: Ingredient costs jumped. What should I change?
cafe.page_title: Cafe cost decision — three choices compared
cafe.headline: Ingredient costs are up {shock}%. What should you do?
cafe.hero_lede: Three ways to respond, compared on the same model of your cafe and the same assumptions. Only the decision changes between them.
cafe.what_changed: Your suppliers put ingredient prices up {shock}%.

world_verdict_labels.C: A 5% rise plus simplifying the menu

cafe.unknown_why: Everything here turns on how many customers you lose when the price goes up. Nobody knows that number for your cafe — the figure used comes from research on eating out as a whole.
cafe.unknown_how: Raise the price of a few items for at least two weeks, and every day count them and a few unchanged items. It may still leave the answer open — that is worth knowing too.

sens_help.low: Loyal customers, or your competitors are raising prices too.
sens_help.central: The typical response found in research on eating out.
sens_help.high: Stress case: competitors hold their prices and customers have easy alternatives.

cafe.c_card_note: Depends on how much simplifying the menu cuts ingredient cost (about {red} points here) and how many {unit} leave with the removed items ({loss}%). Neither is measured from your cafe.
cafe.chart_lede: Costs take about a week to rise — you are still using stock bought at the old price. Customers take a couple of weeks to react to a new price.
cafe.sources_note: Research gives a reference range for eating out as a whole. Your own customers may be more or less price-sensitive than that.
limits_does_not: Know how your individual customers will behave.
Model the wider economy, seasons or new customers.

shop.question: My supplier raised prices. Should I pass it on?
shop.page_title: Shop cost decision — three choices compared
shop.headline: Your supplier put prices up {shock}%. Should you pass it on?
shop.hero_lede: Three ways to respond, compared on the same model of your shop and the same assumptions. Only the decision changes between them.
shop.what_changed: Your supplier put wholesale prices up {shock}%.

world_verdict_labels.C: A 4% rise plus dropping low-margin lines

shop.unknown_why: A shop's customers can often buy the same item elsewhere, so a price rise costs more orders here than in a trade where people come for you specifically. How much more is the thing nobody has measured for your shop.
shop.unknown_how: Put prices up on a handful of lines for at least two weeks and compare them with lines you left alone. Numbers from the last time you raised prices help too, if nothing else changed at the same time.

sens_help.low: Loyal customers, an awkward shop to replace, or competitors raising prices too.
sens_help.central: Our judgement: customers who could shop elsewhere, with some effort.
sens_help.high: The research figure for customers who can buy the identical item elsewhere.

shop.c_card_note: Depends on how much dropping low-margin lines cuts your cost of goods (about {red} points here) and how many {unit} leave with those lines ({loss}%). Neither is measured from your shop.
shop.chart_lede: Costs take about three weeks to rise — the stock on your shelves was bought at the old price. Customers react to a new price within a week or two.
shop.sources_note: The research quoted measures customers switching between brands on the same shelf, which is easier than switching shops. It sets the top of the range rather than the middle.
limits_does_not: Know how your individual customers will behave.
Model competitors, marketplaces or search ranking.

salon.page_title: Salon pricing decision — three choices compared
salon.headline: Your diary is {shock}% busier. Is it time to raise prices?

salon.what_changed: Demand for appointments is up {shock}%, and your diary has a ceiling.

world_verdict_labels.C: A 5% rise plus shifting the mix

salon.unknown_why: There is no published figure for how salon clients respond to a price rise — not a weak one, none we could use honestly. Every setting on this control is our judgement, so your own test is worth more here than in any other trade.
salon.unknown_how: Raise the price of one service, or for new clients only, and over six weeks compare requests and rebookings with services you left alone.

sens_help.low: A loyal client base who book with you personally.
sens_help.central: Our judgement for an appointment business with real switching costs.
sens_help.high: Stress case: clients who treat it as a commodity and shop on price.

salon.capacity_note: Your diary has a ceiling, so some of the {unit} a price rise costs you were being turned away anyway. That is why raising prices costs less here than the price sensitivity alone suggests.
salon.c_card_note: Depends on how much shifting the mix cuts your cost per appointment (about {red} points here), how much it lifts the average ticket, and how many {unit} leave with the discounts ({loss}%). None is measured from your salon.
salon.chart_lede: Clients on a six-week cycle only meet a new price at their next visit, so the reaction arrives over a couple of weeks rather than at once.
salon.sources_note: We found no published figure for personal-care services that could be used honestly. Every setting on the price control is our judgement. The retail studies listed are only the reference points our range was positioned against.
limits_does_not: Know how your individual clients will behave.
Model hiring, longer hours or a second chair.

A.good: Prices stay put and clients are happy
A.bad: but you fill up and start turning appointments away

salon.experiment: Put the price of one or two in-demand services up {rise}, or for new clients only. Count requests for them — not bookings, which your diary caps — and requests for your other services, for two weeks before and at least four weeks after.
